name: Testosterone enanthate

track.title: Approved outside the US
track.line: Testoviron and others in 10 EU states

what.text: Testosterone enanthate is an ester of testosterone, in oil. Attaching the ester makes it last longer in the body; it is broken down to free testosterone after injection. In the US it comes as an injection into the muscle (generic vials) and as Xyosted, a weekly autoinjector placed under the skin.
How it acts, according to the FDA labels:

items.text: Testosterone drives the growth of the male sex organs and keeps up male traits such as beard and body hair, a deeper voice, and muscle and fat distribution.
Testosterone from outside the body lowers the brain’s release of LH. At large doses it can also lower FSH and suppress sperm production.

what.text: Testosterone enanthate is approved for men with hypogonadism caused by a medical condition. Safety and efficacy in men whose testosterone is low only because of age have not been established.

research.text: Xyosted was approved on open-label trials that measured hormone levels in men with hypogonadism. The best-known older study of testosterone enanthate is a WHO trial that used weekly injections as a male contraceptive. It shows clearly what the drug does to sperm production.

research.title: Xyosted 52-week study (Kaminetsky et al.)

facts.v: Xyosted 75 mg under the skin once a week, adjusted to 50, 75 or 100 mg
average testosterone over the weekly interval at week 12; peaks; side effects

research.found: The label reports 90% of men with an average testosterone in the normal range (300 to 1,100 ng/dL) at week 12; the journal paper reports 92.7%. No man had a peak above 1,500 ng/dL at week 12 on the label’s count. Raised hematocrit, high blood pressure and raised PSA were the most common side effects and led 30 men to stop. Antares Pharma, the maker, employed one author.

research.title: WHO male contraception study

facts.v: multicentre study, 10 centres in 7 countries, no placebo
testosterone enanthate 200 mg by injection into the muscle every week
up to 6 months to suppress sperm, then a 12-month efficacy phase
sperm counts, pregnancies in partners, recovery after stopping

research.found: 157 men had no sperm in 3 samples in a row (65% at 6 months; mean time 120 days). In the efficacy phase there was 1 pregnancy in 1,486 months. After injections stopped, the median time to recover a sperm count of at least 20 million/mL was 3.7 months. This is an experimental use, not an approved one.

src.label: WHO Task Force on methods for the regulation of male fertility, Lancet

research.title: Autoinjector drug-level study (Kaminetsky et al.)

facts.v: dose-finding, open-label, parallel-group; men randomized to 2 doses
39 men with hypogonadism; a reference group stayed on 200 mg injections into the muscle
testosterone enanthate 50 mg or 100 mg under the skin once a week by autoinjector
testosterone levels over the weekly interval; safety

research.found: Both doses kept average testosterone in the normal range over the week. Mean steady-state testosterone at week 6 was 422 ng/dL on 50 mg and 896 ng/dL on 100 mg. The authors reported no clinically significant side effects. One author worked for Antares Pharma, the maker.

research.text: The generic label is an older-format label without new animal data. It states that testosterone from outside the body inhibits LH, and at large doses FSH, through feedback on the pituitary.

us.text: Testosterone enanthate is FDA approved. The first approval was Delatestryl, in December 1953; Xyosted, a weekly autoinjector, was approved in September 2018. It is a Schedule III controlled substance. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: NDA 209863 (Antares Pharma), approved September 28, 2018. Approved for testosterone replacement in adult men with primary or hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
Delatestryl, NDA 009165, approved December 24, 1953, is now listed as discontinued. Generic injections are approved, for example ANDA 091120 (Hikma, 2012).

items.text: the generic label also lists delayed puberty in carefully selected boys, and advanced breast cancer in some women, as approved uses.
both labels say safety and efficacy have not been established in men with age-related hypogonadism. Use outside the labeled conditions is off-label.

on February 28, 2025, FDA told makers of all testosterone products to add TRAVERSE results, remove boxed-warning language on heart outcomes, and add or update blood pressure warnings. The Xyosted label now includes TRAVERSE data. The Hikma generic label checked still says long-term heart safety trials have not been done, while also warning about blood pressure.

world.lead: Testosterone enanthate is an approved prescription medicine in the US, Canada, Northern Ireland and 10 EU member states. Canada’s only marketed product is a generic injection; Delatestryl was cancelled there in December 2025. It is banned in sport at all times.

countries.status: Approved medicine (Delatestryl, 1953, discontinued; generic injections; Xyosted autoinjector, 2018) for male hypogonadism. Prescription-only; Schedule III.

Authorised medicine: a generic testosterone enanthate injection (Hikma), marketed since January 2024, listed as a controlled drug (CDSA Schedule IV). Delatestryl was cancelled post-market in December 2025.

after.text: Australia’s Poisons Standard (October 2026) lists testosterone in Schedule 4 (prescription only) and in Appendix D, clause 5, for anabolic and androgenic steroids, which must not be possessed without authority under local law. The TGA’s register could not be reached to confirm which products are registered.

after.title: Sport
after.text: Testosterone is named under class S1.1, anabolic androgenic steroids, on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List, when given from outside the body; the class covers its esters. S1 is prohibited at all times (in and out of competition) and its substances are non-Specified. Testosterone stays named in S1.1 on the 2027 list, in force January 1, 2027.

side.text: Testosterone enanthate has testosterone’s class risks: raised red cell counts, blood clots, higher blood pressure, prostate effects and suppressed sperm production. In the WHO study, weekly injections stopped sperm production in most healthy men; it came back after stopping.

items.text: Xyosted raised average systolic/diastolic blood pressure by 3.9/1.5 mm Hg after 12 weeks. High blood pressure was reported in 12.7% of men in the 1-year study. In TRAVERSE, a trial of testosterone gel, major heart events were 7% vs 7.3% on placebo.

raised hematocrit was the most common side effect of Xyosted in the 1-year study (14.0%). A rise in red cell mass may raise the risk of blood clots. Clots in the legs and lungs have been reported with testosterone enanthate.

reduced fertility is seen in some men on testosterone, and the Xyosted label says the effect may be irreversible. In the WHO study, 65% of healthy men had no sperm by 6 months; sperm counts recovered after a median of 3.7 months off injections.

src.label: WHO Task Force on methods for the regulation of male fertility, Lancet

items.text: raised PSA (12.0%) and prostatitis were reported with Xyosted. Older men may have a higher risk of an enlarged prostate and prostate cancer on androgens. Testosterone must not be used by men with breast cancer or known or suspected prostate cancer.
the Xyosted label warns that depression, suicidal thoughts and behaviour, including completed suicide, occurred in its trials.

injection site bruising and bleeding, headache and back pain were common with Xyosted. The generic label lists breast growth, acne, more frequent or prolonged erections, changes in libido, swelling, liver effects (including rare liver tumours and peliosis hepatis with long high-dose use) and, rarely, allergic reactions.

in children it can close the growth plates early and reduce adult height. It must not be used in pregnancy, because it can masculinize a female fetus. Abuse at high doses has caused serious heart and mental health effects.

unconfirmed: The TGA’s register could not be reached, so Australian product registrations were not confirmed.
Great Britain (outside Northern Ireland) was not checked on the MHRA’s own product register.
Drugs@FDA’s web pages redirected automated requests; approval dates come from FDA’s openFDA copy of Drugs@FDA.
surprises: The Hikma generic testosterone enanthate label on DailyMed (May 2026) still says long-term heart safety trials have not been done, unlike the Xyosted label, which includes the TRAVERSE results FDA asked all makers to add in 2025.
Delatestryl, the first US testosterone enanthate brand (1953), is discontinued in the US and was cancelled in Canada in December 2025.
